info.bio: Heart es una banda de rock que surgió del Bellevue, un suburbio de Seattle, Washington, y Vancouver, Columbia Británica. Pasando por varios cambios de alineación, la única constante de los miembros del grupo son las hermanas Ann y Nancy Wilson. El grupo saltó a la fama en la década de 1970 con su música influenciada por elementos como el rock duro de Led Zeppelin, así como por la música folk. Han vendido más de 30 millones de álbumes en todo el mundo.

podcast.title: Ann Wilson's Experience with Sexism in Radio
podcast.body: Ann Wilson recounted that many times in their 20s, they would encounter radio station personnel who would make comments like, "we love your tits." She described this as irritating and any physical touch as "icky, nauseating." She also noted that in the 70s, complaining about such behavior would likely result in her own termination. "Many times in our 20s we'd go into radio stations and they'd say, we love your tits. It was irritating."

podcast.title: Breakthrough and Mainstream Success
podcast.body: Heart's legitimate rock band breakthrough coincided with the late 70s evolution of rock, blowing up in the 1980s with arena rock and power ballads. Their 1985 self-titled album, `Heart`, marked their mainstream success by going to number one and producing four Top 10 hits, despite a shift towards a more sentimental sound. "Hearts breakthrough as a legitimate rock band coincided with this evolution of rock and roll that began to build up steam in the late 70s and totally blew up in the 1980s."

podcast.title: Influence on Grunge
podcast.body: Heart was a key influence, alongside Led Zeppelin and Black Sabbath, that crossbred with punk/hardcore in the Pacific Northwest to eventually become Grunge. This unexpected cross-pollination was a result of the unique touring challenges posed by the Rocky Mountains, which made it easier for bands to play local punk shows in the Seattle area than major touring acts. "And that's how it crossbred with Led Zeppelin and Black Sabbath and Hart. To eventually become Grunge, that would not have happened without the Rocky Mountains being in the way."

podcast.title: Internal Turmoil and Image Makeover
podcast.body: The band's situation was complicated by internal turmoil, and they felt pressure to undergo a "makeover" to sell records and get radio play in the 1980s. This led to a sound distinct from their earlier classic rock hits. "Hearts situation was not helped by some of the inner turmoil within the band, but they were also in a situation where selling records and getting on the radio, which still went hand in hand in the 80s, required a makeover."

podcast.body: Mushroom Records overtly sexualized sisters Ann and Nancy Wilson to promote their album `Dreamboat Annie`. The album cover showed them with bare shoulders standing back to back, and the label took out a full-page ad in Rolling Stone magazine with the caption, "It was only our first time." "Mushroom records, which does not exist anymore, was not above completely sexualizing and enancy who are sisters to sell the record."

xref.title: Nash the Slash (Jeff Plunman, Toronto, 1948–2014) – Surgical Bandages Adopted After Three Mile Island Accident (1979); David Gilmour Offered Guitar Part but Nash Refused All Guitars
xref.body: Nash the Slash's real name was Jeff Plunman, born in Toronto on March 26, 1948. The stage name came from a character in a 1927 Laurel and Hardy silent film. He co-founded the prog band FM in 1975 and audiences could see his face briefly, but after the nuclear accident at Three Mile Island near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania in March 1979, Nash adopted surgical bandages that completely obscured his face as a way of raising awareness about what could happen if a nuclear plant melted down. He left FM around 1980 to resume his solo career, toured with Gary Numan and the Tubes, hung out with Iggy Pop and Daniel Lanois, and Brian Eno collaborated on his records. David Gilmour of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs — but Nash refused because he never used guitars on any of his songs. He made records until 2012, was especially popular in Germany and Poland, and died of an apparent heart attack at his Toronto home on May 10, 2014, at age 66. His music and costumes are managed by the Nash the Slash Legacy organization and much was donated to the National Music Center in Calgary. His best-known record was 1984's American Bandages. "David Gilmore of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs, but Nash refused because he never, ever used guitars on any of his songs."

xref.title: Berlin Regeneration and Routine (Late 1976)
xref.body: In West Berlin, David Bowie rented an apartment at 155 Hauptstrasse in the Schöneberg district, situated above a car repair shop. He established a routine that included having breakfast at a gay bar next door and exploring the city's unique areas by walking or biking. Following a heart attack scare in the fall of 1976, both Bowie and Iggy Pop began to earnestly clean up their lifestyles, leading to a period of intense creativity. "Apparently, Bowie also had a big thing for Hitler and spent a lot of his time touring World War II sites."

xref.title: Regeneration in West Berlin (May 1976)
xref.body: In late May 1976, Iggy Pop moved to West Berlin with David Bowie to escape their destructive lifestyles in Los Angeles and to regenerate among the city's diverse community of bohemians, weirdos, drug addicts, prostitutes, and transsexuals. This move, prompted by Bowie's heart attack scare in the fall of 1976, led both artists to seriously clean up their acts and embark on an incredibly creative period. "So in late May 1976, Bowie and Iggy moved to West Berlin to regenerate in the company of the Bohemians and weirdos and drug addicts and prostitutes and transsexuals who lived there."

xref.title: Discovery of Death (1979)
xref.body: On the morning of February 2nd, 1979, his mother discovered Sid Vicious stone-cold dead in bed next to Michelle Robinson. The heroin he had taken the night before was apparently 99% pure, and his detoxed body was unable to cope. As he slept, his heart beat slower and slower, and his lungs filled up with fluid, leading to his death. "February 2nd, 1979, Groundhog Day, Sid's mum comes into check on her boy and he's lying in bed next to Michelle. And he was stone-cold dead."

xref.title: Fatal Heroin Overdose – February 2, 1979
xref.body: The night before his trial, on February 1, 1979, Sid attended a party in his honor at his new girlfriend Michelle Robinson's home, with his mother and friends present. His mother supplied him with heroin, and later he took more from her purse. He overdosed and was put to bed around 3 AM. No doctor was called to avoid violating his bail conditions. The next morning, he was found dead, naked, on top of the covers.

xref.title: Death by Cocaine Overdose (October 21, 1995)
xref.body: Shannon Hoon died on October 21, 1995, at the age of 28, from a heart attack brought on by a cocaine overdose. Despite Blind Melon's debut album going platinum four times over and a hit single, Shannon struggled with drug and alcohol issues, attempting rehab at least twice without success, against the advice of his drug counselor. The band had just finished recording their second album, "Soup," and had begun an 18-month tour on September 19, 1995. Following a disappointing show in Houston on October 20, Shannon went on an all-night drug binge. The band arrived in New Orleans early on October 21 to play Tipitina's. Shannon called his girlfriend for 45 minutes, explaining how "messed up" he was, then visited Smoothie King on Canal Street and spent 45 minutes talking to someone on a psychic hotline. He went back to the tour bus instead of the hotel, laid down in bandmate Christopher Thorn's bunk, and was found unresponsive by a sound technician at 1:30 PM. EMS declared him dead. "He was twenty-eight. He's buried in Dayton Cemetery in Dayton, Indiana, and the epitaph is from a blind million song called Change."

xref.title: Discovery of Death (1995)
xref.body: On the bus, Shannon undressed and lay down in bandmate Christopher Thorn's bunk, with two sound technicians also asleep on board. At 1:30 PM, one of the technicians tried to wake him for sound check, but Shannon was unresponsive. The bus driver called an ambulance while the tour manager initiated CPR. Upon arrival, EMS declared Shannon Hoon dead at the age of 28, attributing his death to a heart attack caused by a cocaine overdose. "At one thirty then afternoon, one of those texts tried to wake Shannon up for a sound check. But Shannon wouldn't wake up."

xref.title: Final Hours in New Orleans (October 21, 1995)
xref.body: After an all-night drug binge following a disappointing Houston show, Shannon Hoon arrived in New Orleans with Blind Melon early on October 21, 1995, to play a club show at Tipitina's. While the rest of the group checked into a hotel, Shannon chose to go for a walk. He made a 45-minute call to his girlfriend, describing his "messed up" state, then visited a Smoothie King on Canal Street, and spent another 45 minutes talking on a psychic hotline. Instead of joining the band at the hotel, he returned to the tour bus, got undressed, and lay down in bandmate Christopher Thorn's bunk. He was found unresponsive at 1:30 PM by a sound technician attempting to wake him for sound check, and EMS declared him dead of a heart attack caused by a cocaine overdose. "While he was there, he apparently spent 45 minutes talking to somebody on a psychic hotline. When he hung up, he went back to the bus, instead of checking into the hotel with everybody else."

xref.title: Shannon Hoon's Overdose Death (1995)
xref.body: Lead singer Shannon Hoon died on October 21, 1995, from a massive cocaine overdose on the band's tour bus. The bus was parked in a parking lot outside the Hotel Intercontinental in downtown New Orleans. The night before, Blind Melon had played a "bad show" in Houston, with Hoon "buzzed on Coke" for most of the gig, and he continued using his stash on the bus to New Orleans. He was last seen around 10 AM after having breakfast, before creeping back into guitarist Christopher Thorne's bunk, where he was found unresponsive shortly after noon. "The official coroner's verdict? Heart failure brought about by a massive cocaine overdose. The date was October 21, 1995."

xref.title: Big Day Out Tragedy and Lawsuits (2001)
xref.body: As headliners at the Big Day Out festival in Sydney on January 21, 2001, Limp Bizkit's singer Fred Durst had pre-show concerns about inadequate security barriers, which he discussed multiple times with the promoter. Despite assurances, a massive crush occurred towards the stage during their first song, resulting in approximately 30 injuries and the death of 15-year-old Jessica Milicic, who died five days later from a heart attack caused by asphyxiation. An investigation closed in November 2002 without charges, but new security rules were implemented. Milicic's parents filed a civil suit against Limp Bizkit in November 2004, and the band was also sued by their own insurance company over legal fees, leading to speculation that these events contributed to their subsequent quiet period. "So, is it any wonder we haven't heard anything from Limpbiscat since then?"

xref.title: Dave Williams' Death on Tour (2002)
xref.body: On August 14, 2002, during Ozzfest, Drowning Pool's lead singer Dave Williams was found dead in his bunk on the tour bus, having died in his sleep. His death was attributed to cardiomyopathy, a disorder affecting the heart muscle often caused by viral infections or high blood pressure, thus determined to be from natural causes. The band later released a memorial DVD, with proceeds directed towards achieving Williams' dream of buying his parents a house. "He died of something called cardiomyopathy, a disorder that affects the heart muscle caused by things like viral infections or high blood pressure."

xref.body: During his Prague concert on June 23, 2004, David Bowie's performance was severely affected by his heart attack. After an attempt to play "Station to Station" which started and stopped, everyone left the stage. Ten minutes later, Bowie and the band returned to try and finish the song, then performed "The Man Who Sold the World," but "Changes" ended after its intro, effectively concluding the show. xref.title: Pandrogyny Project – Matching Breast Implants on Valentine's Day 2005 with Life Partner Lady Jaye
xref.body: Genesis P-Orridge, founder of Throbbing Gristle (who coined the term "industrial music" with their 1977 debut *The Second Annual Report*) and later Psychic TV, entered into a relationship with Psychic TV keyboardist Lady Jaye Breyer that was itself conceived as an ongoing performance art piece. The goal was to make the two people look increasingly alike through shared wardrobes, matching haircuts, permanent eyeliner, lip injections, oral surgeries, cheek implants, and ultimately matching breast implants, received together on Valentine's Day 2005. Their shared identity was to be called Ms. Breyer P-Orridge — a merged being making a statement about the oneness of humanity and the obsolescence of traditional gender roles. Genesis retained his original genitalia; Lady Jaye declined to have anything added. Lady Jaye died on October 9, 2007, from a previously undiagnosed heart condition possibly connected to her long-term battle with stomach cancer. "Their goal was to merge their identities into a single being."

xref.title: Taylor Hawkins' Death (March 25, 2022)
xref.body: Foo Fighters drummer Taylor Hawkins died suddenly on March 25, 2022, in Bogota, Colombia, just before the band was set to headline a festival. At approximately 7:40 PM on that Friday night, a call was made from a Four Seasons property reporting a guest with severe chest pains, but EMS responders arrived too late. Officially, he died from complications related to an enlarged heart (cardiomegaly), which weighed 600 grams (compared to a normal 300 grams). Although his doctors were aware of his enlarged heart for years, attributing it to his active lifestyle of surfing, biking, and intense drumming, little other information regarding his death was released, due to an "airtight" news blackout imposed by the band and management. This lack of information fueled conspiracy theories, though sources suggested a congenital problem exacerbated by exhaustion, as Hawkins had reportedly been feeling "rough" in the months leading up to the South American tour. His death profoundly impacted Dave Grohl, the Foo Fighters, and millions of fans globally. "Taylor was dead. Officially, he died of complications involving an enlarged heart, something called cardiomagalley."

xref.title: Alan Rankine Death (January 2, 2023) – Heart Disease, Age 64; Launched Snow Patrol, Belle & Sebastian, Biffy Clyro via Electric Honey Records
xref.body: Alan Rankine co-founded the Associates with Billy MacKenzie in Dundee, Scotland in 1979 — evolving out of post-punk bands and following a Bowie-like direction. A former competitive tennis player (too short at 5'8" to go professional), Rankine also worked as a production collaborator with the Cocteau Twins. After the Associates broke up, he became a lecturer at Stow College in Glasgow teaching music production, and helped students set up a record label called Electric Honey, which launched Snow Patrol, Belle & Sebastian, and Biffy Clyro. He was diagnosed with heart disease in the 2020s and died at home with family on January 2, 2023, at age 64. "He helped him set up a record label called Electric Honey, and that label launched the careers of bands like Snow Patrol, Bell and Sebastian, and Biffy Clyro."

When he had a fatal heart attack, he died right there."

xref.title: Father's Diverse Ventures and Tragic Death
xref.body: Hugh Everett III successfully applied mathematics, specifically Lagrange multipliers, to become a millionaire. He then used some of his wealth to establish a company focused on studying the parallels between human speech and machine speech. Sadly, he died of a heart attack in 1982, and his son Mark was the one who found him. "Later, Mr. Everett applied mathematics to making money."

xref.title: Formation Date and Naming
xref.body: The closest estimate for The Clash's formation date is June 6, 1976. During rehearsals, the group considered various names such as The Mirrors, The Outsiders, The Psychotic Negatives, The Phones, The Heart Drops, and The Weak Heart Drops. The name "Clash" was ultimately chosen after the bass player read a newspaper headline describing a "Clash with police." "The closest we can come down to nailing a date for the Clash's formation is June 6th, 1976."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation History
xref.body: Joe, the guitarist for The 101ers, was profoundly influenced by the Sex Pistols' attitude and energy when they opened for his band at the Nashville club, despite their "awful" musicianship. A few days later, Joe left The 101ers and began forming a new band with others who admired the Sex Pistols. This new group went through several name changes—The Psychotic Negatives, The Weak Heart Drops, The Outsiders, The Mirrors in the Evening Standards—before finally settling on The Clash. "It was their attitude and their energy that grabbed his attention."

xref.title: Frontman's Death Coincides with Band Name
xref.body: The lead singer of The Cardiacs, British musician Tim Smith, died from a heart attack, creating a notable and unusual coincidence with the band's name. "Tim Smith, a British musician, died this year. It was a heart attack, what strange is that Tim was the lead singer of a band called The Cardiacs."

xref.title: Healing Process and Return to Music
xref.body: It took Josh Homme a couple of years to mentally recover from his traumatic experiences, utilizing meditation as part of his healing. He was cleared to walk again in December 2010, and by January 2011, he began working on a new Queens of the Stone Age album, though he initially struggled as his "heart just wasn't in it." "It took a couple of years to sort out his head. He created his meditation as being part of the healing process. The depression he says was absolutely intense. Eventually, Josh got back to being something of his old self. He was clear to start walking again in December 2010, and in January 2011, he started working on a new Queen's of the Stone Age album."

"And that's how it crossbred with Led Zeppelin and Black Sabbath and Hart. To eventually become Grunge, that would not have happened without the Rocky Mountains being in the way."

xref.body: In July 2008, longtime Blink-182 producer Jerry Finn had just completed his work on a Morrissey album shortly before suffering a cerebral hemorrhage and a massive heart attack, which ultimately led to his death. xref.title: Joe Strummer's Cause of Death
xref.body: Joe Strummer died on December 22nd, 2002, from an intra-mural coronary artery, a rare genetic condition where a main blood vessel of the heart grows within the muscle wall, eventually squeezing shut and causing a fatal heart attack. "The cause of death was an intra-mural coronary artery."

xref.title: Joey Ramone's Marfan Syndrome
xref.body: Jeffrey Hyman (Joey Ramone) suffered from Marfan Syndrome, an inherited disorder affecting connective tissue, leading to his tall, gangly physique with long limbs and fingers. This condition can also cause serious heart problems and, if untreated, typically limits life expectancy to 32 years. "Young Jeffrey grew up with all sorts of health problems. He was tall and gauky as the result of something called Marfan Syndrome, which is an inherited disorder living on chromosome 15 that messes with connective tissue."

xref.body: Singer Blake Schwarzenbach's creative process involved initially pouring his heart out into personal journals, then transforming those intimate thoughts and feelings into songs. This method created a profound connection with fans who deeply identified with his lyrics. "First, he poured his heart out into personal journals. xref.title: Later Career and Influence
xref.body: Moondog was taken seriously as a performer and composer, eventually securing a recording contract for multiple albums. He married, started a family, and returned to Carnegie Hall in 1989 to conduct a performance of his own works. He later moved to Europe, where he died of heart failure in 1999 at age 83. His life and music were inspirational to various artists, from hippies to bands important to the creation of Trip Hop. "Moon Dog eventually found his way to Europe where he died of heart failure in 1999 at the age of 83."

xref.title: Later Decline and Death
xref.body: In 2003, Fisher experienced a six-month episode of paranoia that led him back to homelessness. His aunt rescued him and helped him get back on his medication, which restored some functionality but also stifled his musical creativity, leading him to stop performing. He died in June 2011 from heart failure. "But the medications somehow snuffed out his musical creativity, and he never performed again."

xref.title: Marfan Syndrome Diagnosis
xref.body: Joey also had Marfan Syndrome, a genetic disorder affecting connective tissue. This condition often results in individuals being very tall and thin with long limbs, fingers, and toes, and can lead to scoliosis and certain heart and circulatory issues. The syndrome's characteristic height made his fall more dangerous, contributing to the severity of his injuries. "People with Marfan's tend to be very tall and very thin with long limbs, fingers and toes."

As their groups evolved into Heart, Nancy increasingly focused on hard rock and discovered drop D tuning, a technique that would become vital to the grunge era 15 years later. The 5,100-square-foot residence featured direct elevator access, 11-foot ceilings, a large library, four bedrooms, four bathrooms, and three terraces. xref.body: The tour supporting the album "When Your Heart Stop's Beating" was a highlight for Mark Hoppus and Travis Barker (members of Plus 44), providing them the opportunity to play small clubs again after a long time, which was a re-energizing experience. She subsequently made a series of suicide attempts, including one where she tried to stab herself in the heart but the knife got stuck in her sternum. "Then came a series of suicide attempts. xref.body: Halsey has Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS), a heart condition that causes the heart to beat excessively fast merely by standing up. Symptoms include brain fog, fatigue, headaches, shaking, and even purple discoloration of the feet when upright. "And she has postural, orthostatic, tachycardia syndrome. That's a heart problem that can send the thing beating way too fast just by standing up. It results in brain fog, fatigue, headaches, shaking and even having your feet turned purple when you stand up."

xref.title: Priesthood Calling Abandoned for Guitar Amplifier – Jack White's Near-Seminary Life
xref.body: Jack White (born John Anthony Gillis) is the youngest of ten children of Gorman and Theresa Gillis, a devout Catholic couple in Detroit. Both parents worked for the Catholic Archdiocese of Detroit — his mother as a secretary, his father in maintenance. Jack served as an altar boy at the Church of the Holy Redeemer and, following in the footsteps of his six brothers, developed a sense of religious calling. He applied to and was accepted at a seminary in Wisconsin, but had a last-second change of heart when he realized he would not be permitted to bring his new guitar amplifier. He enrolled in public school instead. Had he gone, there would have been no White Stripes, no marriage and divorce to Meg White, and no subsequent marriage to model Karen Elson. "So talk about a decision that changes your life, huh?"

xref.title: Proposed Cause of Death: Cardiac Episode
xref.body: In the opinion of the speaker, Taylor Hawkins died of a cardiac episode brought on by a previously diagnosed enlarged heart, which doctors were aware of but not concerned about, attributing it to years of intense drumming, mountain biking, and surfing, dubbing it a "runner's heart." "And in my opinion, he died of some kind of cardiac episode brought on by a previously diagnosed enlarged heart. A doctor knew all about it, but he wasn't worried, saying that all that heart muscle was the result of many years of intense drumming, plus mountain biking and surfing. They called this a runner's heart."

xref.body: An alternative cover for Depeche Mode's *Music for the Masses* was created, featuring a stylized megaphone in a white and orange motif with drawn sound waves. "About 135 copies were prepared for shipping to stores, but then the band and the label had a change of heart and had all those copies recalled."

xref.title: Sudden Cardiac Death and Implanted Defibrillator
xref.body: Aaron Lazar, lead singer of The Giraffes, experienced sudden cardiac death one night while driving his girlfriend home, causing him to slump over the steering wheel. He was later told that his heart had stopped twice. This condition is not a heart attack but a malfunction in the brain's signal to the heart, with only a 5% survival rate. Lazar now has an implanted defibrillator that shocks his heart back to life if it stops. "He was diagnosed with something called sudden cardiac death. This is not a heart attack. Something goes wrong with the signal from your brain that tells your heart to keep beating. Only 5% of people with this condition survive. Aaron ended up with an implant at defibrillator."

xref.title: Suspicion of Murder Despite Suicide Note
xref.body: Despite a suicide note and a history of ADHD, depression, suicidal ideation, drug use, and heavy drinking, police, the coroner, and fans remained suspicious of Elliot Smith's death. The primary reason for this suspicion was the absence of "hesitation wounds," as he had stabbed himself cleanly twice directly in the heart. "Police were still suspicious. xref.title: Therapeutic Effects of Music
xref.body: Dr. Mark Tramos compared AC/DC's music to a "chemo drug" in a music therapy study conducted at Harvard. The band's riffs, beats, melodies, and simple lyrics are noted for hitting all the targets required for therapeutic effect. Listening to AC/DC can improve heart rate and blood pressure, regulate and boost muscle activity, and enhance athletic performance, strength, endurance, and power. Furthermore, surgeons who listen to AC/DC while operating are reported to make fewer mistakes due to the music encouraging focus. For cancer patients, prescribed AC/DC music can significantly reduce anxiety and pain, thereby improving the effectiveness of other medications. "Dr. Mark Tramos says that ACDC can act like a chemo drug. The riffs, the beats, the melodies, and simple lyrics seem to hit all the targets."

"A preliminary toxicology report said that there were 10 different substances in Taylor's system, ranging from weed and opioids to antidepressants."

xref.title: Tragic Death
xref.body: Michael Been passed away on August 19th, 2010, at the age of 60, due to a fatal heart attack. He was working as a soundman for his son Robert's band, Black Rebel Motorcycle Club, at a festival in Brussels when the incident occurred. "On August 19th of 2010, Dad was working as a soundman for his son's band, a festival in Brussels. When he had a fatal heart attack, he died right there. He was just 60."

xref.title: Tragic Suicide
xref.body: Mark Linkous's battle with depression persisted despite his continued musical work. While in the process of divorcing his wife of 19 years, he took his own life in Knoxville, Tennessee. He used a rifle, aiming it at his heart, and at the time of his death, he had a blood alcohol level of .43, with various antidepressants and anti-anxiety medications found in his system. "Then, while on the process of a divorce from his wife of 19 years, he took a rifle, went for a walk, sat down on an alley in Knoxville, Tennessee, aimed the gun at his heart and pulled the trigger."

xref.title: Travis Barker's Cadillac Obsession
xref.body: Travis Barker, the drummer for Blink-182, demonstrates a profound love for Cadillacs, evidenced by numerous tattoos and a substantial car collection. His tattoos include a Chevrolet emblem on his left hand, the 1947 Cadillac logo over his heart, a similar emblem and the cursive "Cadillac" font on his right torso, a 1953 Cadillac on his back, and crossed racing flags with "66" (the year of his favorite Cadillac) on his neck. His multi-million dollar car collection features several Cadillacs, including a 1965 Deville convertible, a 1960 Coupe Deville, and a 1941 Series 62 Deluxe. "Travis has millions of dollars worth of cars, which includes several Caddies, including a 1965 Deville convertible."

xref.title: Underlying Addiction and Private Meltdowns
xref.body: Billy Joe Armstrong's public meltdown at the I Heart Radio Festival in 2012 was a symptom of a deeper, long-standing issue; he had been a "very high functioning addict" since at least 1997. Although he appeared functional outwardly, he admitted that "the other part of my life was falling apart slowly. My foundation was cracked. My endurance in Drake, who saw it." There had been private meltdowns behind the scenes dating back to at least 2009. "Green Day had been working nonstop for years and the workload and the pressure had taken its toll."

xref.body: Joe Strummer's fatal heart condition would not typically be detected through standard medical tests and would only show up during a very proper and in-depth cardiac examination. "This is something that you would never specifically test for."

xref.title: Undiagnosed Congenital Heart Condition (Intramural Coronary Artery)
xref.body: Joe Strummer had an extremely rare, undiagnosed congenital heart condition called an intramural coronary artery, where an errant artery grew through his heart muscle. This condition quietly worsened, eventually constricting the artery and triggering a massive heart attack; only about 100 similar cases have ever been recorded. "He had something called an intramural coronary artery, a congenital condition that quietly got worse. This errant artery grew through the heart muscle. It got bigger and bigger until the artery squeezed shut, triggering a massive heart attack."

xref.title: Unusual Nature of Stab Wounds
xref.body: The method of Elliot Smith's death, two clean stabs directly to the heart without hesitation, is highly unusual for suicide. Statistics indicate that only 4% of suicides involve sharp force trauma, predominantly wrist-slashing. The act of turning a knife sideways and plunging it between the ribs twice without hesitation is considered an extremely painful way to die, fueling theories among fans that "bad drug buddies" might have been involved. "According to statistics on suicide, only 4% of people take their own lives with sharp force trauma and almost all of those involve wrist-slashing."

xref.title: Waco Standoff Playlist
xref.body: Andy Williams's songs were part of the playlist used to bombard the Branch Davidian cult compound in Waco, Texas, in 1993. This tactic was an attempt to break the will of David Koresh and his followers during their prolonged standoff with law enforcement. "That playlist included AQ Breaking Heart by Billy Ray Cyrus, Nancy Sinatra, these boots are made for Wacan, some chanting by Tibetan monks, songs by Andy Williams, and some Christmas sing-alongs by Mitch Miller from the 1950s."

xref.body: Several acoustic versions of Arkells' songs, including "1111," "My Heart's All Yours," and "And Then Some," have become popular choices for first dances at weddings. The band regularly receives emails and videos from couples using their music for these special occasions, considering it a "very cool" and precious recognition. "Like that 1111 acoustic version has been used at like first dances for weddings, like countless times. Same thing with our acoustic versions of my heart, so it's yours.
